items.text: Local commitment and shared governance conflicts in cross-institutional networks constitute an independent knowledge issue; general single-repository ethics literature cannot be equated with having resolved this.

Triangulation of inventories, interviews/documents, and sustained observation can reveal actual decision-making processes and organizational configuration differences, rather than merely aggregating stakeholder opinions.

Empirical issues are integrated with ethical/legal normative arguments, using focus groups and expert discussions to formulate governance recommendations that are usable and adaptable to configurations.

Qualitative case studies and leader introductions may involve selection/power biases; existing opposition sampling and lack of direct donor access necessitate limiting representativeness rather than automatically dismissing the entire project.

Empirical acceptability cannot automatically prove normative legitimacy; traceable fact–norm reasoning, handling of dissent, and applicability conditions across configurations are needed. Having a normative core does not mean no normative analysis has been conducted.

Access, reflexivity, and identity inference risks in embedded observation affect the visibility and credibility of real issues; in addition to two annual field visits, there are ongoing meeting/phone observations, with existing reflection and safeguards.
